text.content:
Rel Astra is older than Hardby and the conspiracy operates here from a position of established authority rather than reactive defense. The Pressure Clock for Phase 4 is shorter (four segments) but the segments hit harder. The party should expect to reach segment 2 or 3 by the end of the phase regardless of what they do; the question is whether segment 4 fires.

The clock at a glance — four escalating rhythms

  1. Polite obstruction — the harbor commission's procedural calendar slows. Records take days instead of hours. Audiences are rescheduled. Halask's filings are docketed in the wrong queue.
  2. Witness pressure — Halask's old Aerdi colleagues become reluctant to discuss the case. A junior partner the party was cultivating receives a transfer offer to Rauxes. Mirelth or Vesh receives a private warning and becomes harder to reach.
  3. Witness loss — one of the party's contacts in Rel Astra is taken or killed. Astor's chandlery is broken into and partially burned (he survives, his records do not) — or the party intercepts it: see the page Optional — The Chandlery Fire (Interceptable), this journal. Or Advocate Thale, prosecuting Lyla, is "reassigned" before Halask can resolve it. Or, in extremis, Halask himself is found dead at the Brass Sextant — Path 1 closes.
  4. The seating proceeds — the harbor commission convenes the candidate vote on the schedule the conspiracy planned, before the party can prevent it. Mirelth is held over (Ruth's procedural objection); Vesh and Tenrel are seated 2-1 on three votes cast, with Reach off the tally under the herald's protocol. The campaign's central stakes have been lost; Phase 4's resolution becomes a question of damage control rather than victory.

Triggers — what advances the clock

TriggerSegments
Arrival under Official Delegation+2 immediate (the delegation was announced by imperial relay long before it arrived; the conspiracy has had the entire crossing to prepare, and used it)
Arrival under Commercial Cover+1 (the conspiracy assumes the party is in the city, prepares for it)
Arrival under Quiet Pursuit+0
The party files an indictment with the Aerdi Commercial Court (Path 1)+1
The party publicly disqualifies Mirelth (Three Seats > Mirelth, option 2)+1
The party briefs Galenix at the Naelax embassy+1 (the embassy leaks the visit within a day)
The party visits Sereth's offices openly more than twice without an audience scheduled+1
The party kills any senior C&V Rel Astra staff member (Path 3, or any escalation)+2 immediate
Each full session day before the filing in which the party makes no investigative progress in Rel Astra+1

The clock stops running on the calendar once the indictment is filed. From the filing onward it advances on events only — a party action from the table above, or a GM-chosen conspiracy move — never on elapsed days. This matters because Path 1's deposition window is weeks long and procedurally protected: the conspiracy cannot simply outwait it, and a party that chose the safest route must not be punished a segment a day for the safety. If the party abandons the filing, or it is struck, the daily trigger resumes. And before the filing, a day spent waiting on a subpoena already served, a deposition already scheduled, or a courier already dispatched is not a day without investigative progress. The trigger is for drift, not for procedure.

Milestones — what happens at each segment

Segment 1 — Polite obstruction

The conspiracy's reaction is procedural and deniable. Records the party requests are "in transit" for three days and arrive incomplete. Audiences are politely rescheduled. Halask's first filing is mis-docketed and requires re-submission. The harbor commission's clerk is suddenly very busy. None of this prevents the party from acting; all of it costs them time. Time advances the clock further.

Segment 2 — Witness pressure

The conspiracy reaches into the party's social and procedural network. Mirelth becomes harder to reach: he leaves Rel Astra for his country estate "for personal reasons" and the disqualification documents must now be served on him by Aerdi rural courier (an additional ten days). Vesh becomes more anxious: his sister-in-law's bond is doubled and the case is moved up on Advocate Thale's calendar. One of Halask's old colleagues declines to provide an expected affidavit. The party can recover from any of these individually; recovering from all of them at once costs Halask one full week of work.

Segment 3 — Witness loss

The conspiracy reaches into the party directly. GM picks one based on what would hurt most:

  • Astor — his chandlery is broken into and partially burned. He survives but his records (signed statements, contact information for the four uncompromised council members) do not. He withdraws from active cooperation. The Old Harbor Ward Council route closes for the rest of the phase.
  • Imperial Advocate Serrin Thale, prosecuting Lyla Vesh, is "reassigned" to a Rauxes posting before Halask can complete the procedural challenge. Vesh's withdrawal becomes contingent on the new advocate, who is harder to predict. Vesh stays on the candidate slate until the matter is resolved; the seating risks proceeding regardless.
  • Sayan (Halask's old colleague) is found drowned in the harbor. The deposition Halask was preparing through her is lost. Halask is shaken. The procedural path slows by another week.
  • Halask himself is found dead at the Brass Sextant. This is the worst single outcome. Path 1 closes entirely. Path 2 becomes the only remaining political option. The party's procedural-court framework dies with Halask. Use this only if the party has been visibly reckless and earned the consequence.

Segment 4 — The seating proceeds

The harbor commission convenes the candidate vote on the schedule the conspiracy planned — the date chosen so that the imperial herald's ceremonial call the following day bars Captain Reach from voting at all. Three votes are cast. Vesh and Tenrel are seated 2-1. Mirelth is held over (Ruth's procedural objection works as planned, but for the conspiracy's benefit, not the party's). The conspiracy's harbor-commission play succeeds. Phase 4's resolution becomes a question of damage control rather than victory.

The party can still indict Sereth after this happens — but the seating cannot be undone for at least two years (the next council confirmation cycle), and the conspiracy now controls the swing votes on every discretionary harbor matter for that period.

If segment 4 fires, the campaign continues into Phase 5 with the conspiracy operationally embedded and the party reduced to documenting its consequences.

How to use the clock at the table

  • Show the players the clock face. Four segments, visible.
  • When you advance, say which trigger fired and what the consequence is.
  • Phase 4's clock is faster than Phase 3's because Rel Astra is denser and the conspiracy is at home. Don't soften the witness loss in segment 3 — that segment is supposed to hurt.
  • The clock should reach 2–3 segments by the end of Phase 4 in a normal-paced campaign. Segment 4 should fire only if the party has been reckless or has refused both procedural and political paths and tried only kinetic ones.

Phase 4 does not name "E." Phase 4 does not even confirm the writer is non-human. It only adds a fourth and a fifth observation to Veska's three from Phase 3, and lets the party assemble a clearer portrait of a hand that does not belong to anyone in the Aerdy realm.

Where the new instances appear

Instance 4 — at the Aerdi imperial registry

If the party investigates the harbor commission's vacancy paperwork through the imperial registry (Halask can arrange access; the registrar is one of his old commercial-court contacts), they will find that the Third Seat vacancy (Lady Mirin Vesh's — the one Tenrel is candidate for) is held open by a single ceremonial succession-deferral, filed by the harbor commission's senior clerk a year and a half ago, within days of the inquest that recorded her fall as an accident. The document itself is unremarkable. The marginal annotation, in a hand the registrar will note he has never seen before, reads: "Sufficient. Hold open until the second autumn after the next." The hand matches Veska's three observations and adds the fourth:

  • Fourth observation: the writer holds the quill in a way that produces uniformly thick downstrokes — implying either a blunted nib used deliberately, or a hand that does not pivot the quill the way Aerdy and Yeomanry hands do. Halask, asked, will recall that some Suel hands write this way, but only certain very old families.
  • And one thing the party cannot have yet. The deferral is filed loose in the open register; the cover that carried its seal is in the registry's sealed-cover file, which the registrar cannot produce for a courtesy visit from an old friend. He will say so, apologetically — and mention in passing, because it stuck in his memory, that the wax on it was "an odd hard black stuff, and not ours." That is a hook, not an observation. The fifth observation is the wax itself, and the party has to earn it on whichever path they are walking. See below.

Instance 5 — the sealing wax (one route on every path)

The fifth observation is the wax, and it is the same observation whichever way the party reaches it: not Aerdi imperial wax (which is a specific recipe of beeswax and pine resin tinted with cinnabar) but something darker and harder that leaves a slight black residue on the paper around the seal. Halask cannot identify it. He has, in his whole career, seen one wax like it — on a single document filed in Aerdi commercial court in 571 by an envoy who claimed to represent "a southern trading concern" that no one ever found again. Give Halask's 571 recollection with the wax, on any path. It is what turns a curiosity into a second data point.

There is a route on each of the three paths. The party gets exactly one of them — whichever their path provides — and one is enough.

  • Path 1 — discovery. Once the indictment is filed, Halask can subpoena the registry's sealed-cover file as an exhibit; a courtesy visit could not open it, a commercial-court order can. The cover arrives among the discovery materials in the second week of depositions, wax intact. This is the quiet way, and it is the reward for having chosen the slow path.
  • Path 2 — Sereth says it himself. Asked directly about the annotations once terms are agreed, Sereth describes the wax on his own correspondence in his own words — "harder than ours, and it leaves a black mark on the paper; my clerk has complained of it for nine years" — and in doing so hands the party the fifth observation, plus the fact that the hand has been on his mail for the better part of a decade and that he has never met its owner and does not expect to. His full answer is quoted in his NPC entry under What Sereth will not concede > The annotation hand. This is the loudest way, and the only one where the villain is the source.
  • Path 3 — the strongroom. In the four minutes the party has before the Aerdi watch arrives, one item in the strongroom is a still-sealed cover in the same hard black wax. Investigation DC 18 to pick it out of the correspondence in the time available. On a failure they take it anyway, unread, in the bundle — Halask identifies it three days later from the seal alone, once they are already at sea, and writes to them about it in Loftwick. The observation is never lost, only delayed. Do not let a bad roll cost the party the thread; let it cost them the moment.

With instance 4 and any one of these three, the party has a portrait of an annotator who is not Aerdi, not Yeomanry, possibly Suel by hand-form, sealing with a wax nobody in Rel Astra can name, operating at the conspiracy's own planning level. They have not named her. They have, however, learned what to look for.

What the party should NOT learn in Phase 4

  • The annotator's name.
  • The annotator's species.
  • The annotator's location.
  • The annotator's organization (House Eilserv, the Vault, Erelhei-Cinlu, Drow politics, the Demon Queen, etc. — none of these surface).
  • That there is more than one annotator. (There is only one, in this conspiracy. Other operators may be visible later.)

What the party SHOULD learn in Phase 4

  • That the conspiracy has a head, and the head is not Sereth, and the head is not in the Aerdy realm.
  • That the head writes — physically writes, with a quill, on paper — and that the writing has identifiable features that can be tracked.
  • That the conspiracy's plans are at least decade-scale, drawn down to the level of which seats become vacant in which months in which years.
  • That the campaign's larger picture is much older than Loftwick, much older than Hardby, and probably much older than the Aerdy realm itself.

How to play this thread at the table

Drip-feed, and keep the two apart. The fourth observation arrives in mid-phase, in the registry research scene, free, from a friendly registrar who does not know what he is handing over. The fifth arrives late — in discovery, in Sereth's office, or out of a bundle carried onto a ship — and it should cost something to get. If both land in the same session the thread reads as a puzzle the party solved; a phase apart, it reads as something that is still going on. Players should leave Phase 4 with a question, not an answer.

If a party somehow reaches the end of the phase with only four observations — no filing, no terms, no strongroom — do not invent a fifth. Have Halask write to them in Loftwick during Phase 5 with the sealed cover he finally pried loose, and let the fifth observation arrive as a letter from a friend two months after they stopped looking. That is a better beat than a tidy count.

GM-only note: The annotator is Eclavdra of House Eilserv, of the Drow city of Erelhei-Cinlu in the deep underdark, currently in the early stages of the long political move that will, decades hence, become the campaign described in Vault of the Drow. The harbor-revenue play in Rel Astra is, for her, a single small piece of a much larger long-term operation: positioning surface-world commercial allies whose continued operation will provide cover and resources for House Eilserv's much slower and much larger move. The descent comes closer and sooner than the Hellfurnaces or the Sulm desert: Phases 7–9 take the party into the route beneath the Cairn Hills. Phase 5 returns them to Loftwick first; Phase 4 itself stays on the surface.

Read aloud at the moment the party leaves Rel Astra. The text below is route-and-resolution-agnostic. Adjust the small details based on the path the party took (indictment filed and trial pending; Sereth resigned; Sereth dead in his office; etc.).

Rel Astra in your last hour does not change. The harbor's clock chimes the seventh bell of morning and every other clock in the city chimes with it, the way Hardby's never quite did. The Aerdi sun is high already. The breeze off the Sea of Gearnat carries the same lemon-and-dust-and-clean-salt smell that the city carried on your first morning, and will carry on every morning until the seas swallow it.

You are leaving. You are leaving with what you came to take, or what you could take, or what was left to be taken after the part you wanted had already been moved.

You carry, in a sealed dispatch case under Halask's procedural seal, a copy of the Aerdi Commercial Court filing that will, sixty days after the preliminary hearing, return Tarlith Vhal Sereth a verdict — or you carry a folded private statement that Sereth signed in his own working office and gave you, in exchange for being allowed to retire to a country estate that has been waiting for him for ten years — or you carry the lead of a hand-written list of the items you were able to recover from the strongroom in the four minutes you had before the Aerdi watch arrived. The shape is different in each case. The weight is the same.

You have left, behind you in the city, the names you have learned. Therion Halask, who will write to Caelith every two weeks for as long as either of them is in office, and who will, in his small careful way, continue to file the procedural motions that keep the conspiracy from finding the easy path it wants. Belven Astor, who will continue to lose 4-3 votes on the Old Harbor Ward Council and continue to bring them. Lord Galenix Naelax, who is now either your ally or your problem, depending on what you chose. The eight others, smaller and more various, whose names you may or may not have learned by the time you left.

You also carry a question. The annotation hand. Five observations, none of them sufficient, all of them recurring. A wax that is not Aerdi imperial wax. A hand that is not Aerdi or Yeomanry or any Suel hand any of you have read. A planning horizon that begins ten years before any of you were attached to this work. Sereth — if you let him speak it — said: "Not from this side of the great desert. I do not know whether the writer is a person, an office, or a guild." Halask, asked the same question, says: "If I had to guess, I would not."

The Lacquer Wave is at the merchant quay, or your carriage is at the Customs Quay, or your horses are at the West Gate stables, or you are leaving on foot through the South Gate. It does not matter which. You are going home.

Caelith's Letter Six is in your pack. You will not read it again on the road. You read it once, twice, three times in your last evening in Rel Astra, and you have remembered the only line you needed to remember: "The conspiracy you have named is not the conspiracy."

The harbor falls behind. The pale walls fall behind. The Old Harbor Ward and the Goldsmiths' Quarter and the Naelax embassy and Sereth's offices and Halask's two rooms above the pastry shop and the Brass Sextant on the third quay — all of it falls behind.

You ride west.

What Phase 4 leaves the party with

  • Sereth's outcome: indicted (Path 1), resigned and exiled (Path 2), or killed (Path 3).
  • The candidate slate: Mirelth withdrawn or disqualified; Vesh withdrawn (if Halask's resolution of Lyla's case completed) or seated (if it did not); Tenrel seated or unseated (depending on whether the indictment or the imperial-seat brief succeeded).
  • The harbor-commission play: stopped for at least two years (Paths 1 or 2 with full intervention); paused for six to twelve months (Path 3); succeeded (segment-4 outcome — campaign continues with the conspiracy operationally embedded).
  • The Aerdy claimant: Galenix briefed and an ally; Galenix unbriefed and an unwitting tool; or Galenix used and now a debtor of the party.
  • The annotation hand: five observations on file — or four, if none of the three routes to the fifth opened, in which case Halask supplies it by letter early in Phase 5 and the read-aloud says "four observations" instead. See The "E." Thread. The writer remains unnamed. The writer has been confirmed to exist and to operate at the conspiracy's planning level.
  • The institutional aftermath: Caelith's standing partially restored or further damaged depending on path; Halask continuing to be a Rel Astra correspondent; Astor continuing to be the party's Rel Astra civic ally.

Where the campaign goes from here — including the answer to the "E." question — is on its own page: GM Only — Where the Campaign Goes From Here, this journal. It is kept separate so that this page can be shown to players without exposing the rest of the module.

An optional kinetic beat for the segment-3 witness-loss milestone. Use it only if you chose "Astor's chandlery broken into and partially burned" as the segment-3 fire, and only if your table would welcome one honest fight in an otherwise procedural phase. Skipping it changes nothing: the milestone resolves off-screen as written.

The telegraph

The conspiracy's fire is set by hired hands, not professionals of the Sarth grade — Rel Astra's commercial quarter is too watched for that. So the job leaks, a little, the evening before: Astor's upstairs neighbour (a retired sailmaker who owes him money and pays it in attention) mentions to Astor that two men in dockers' slops walked the alley behind the chandlery twice at dusk without touching cargo; Astor, being Astor, mentions it to the party in the same breath as an apology for troubling them. If the party has briefed Halask that day, Halask's clerk passes the same rumour from the other direction. The party has one night.

The attempt (third bell after midnight)

Four figures at the alley door of the Wave-and-Anchor: a crew lead (SRD Bandit Captain — a dry, careful woman who has burned three buildings in her life and been paid for two of them), and three Thugs carrying two oil skins, a smoke-pot, and a pry bar (six PCs: a fourth Thug watching the street). Their orders, verbatim, from a voice the lead never saw: "The records room. The whole room. No bodies — bodies bring the imperial watch, and the client is paying for the absence of attention."

They are not fanatics. The lead surrenders if the fight turns — she has no loyalty above her fee — and none of them will kill a downed PC. Calibrated for five PCs at 7th level: a comfortable win the party should feel clever for, not lucky.

Outcomes

  • Intercepted before the oil is lit. The chandlery — and Astor's records — survive. The segment-3 milestone still counts as fired (the conspiracy spent the move), but the witness-loss consequence is cancelled: the Old Harbor Ward Council route stays open. Astor's regard for the party becomes permanent.
  • Intercepted late. The records room burns but the crew is taken; split the difference — Astor loses his older files, keeps the current season, and the Council route survives at one week's delay.
  • The crew lead, taken alive, knows one thing worth having: she was hired by a clerk — young, precise, commercial-court cuffs — who paid in Aerdi scrip and never gave a name. (GM-only: the clerk answers to Tellis Maro, the Cindren-aligned junior advocate who surfaces in Phase 5's Vector D. Do not name Maro; let the description sit in the party's notes until it matches a face.)
  • The party never engages. Run the milestone as written in the Pressure Clock page. No penalty beyond the one already designed.

Pressure Clock: no additional advance for intercepting — the fire itself was the conspiracy's move, not the party's. Killing all four (instead of accepting the surrender) is the only way this beat costs the party: +1 segment, and Astor — who wanted no bodies on his doorstep — is shaken for a week.

pages.name: GM Only — Where the Campaign Goes From Here

text.content:
GM only. Do not show this page to players, and do not read from it at the table. It exists so that the ending read-aloud can be shown or shared without carrying the module's remaining answers with it. Everything below is either a spoiler for Phases 5–9 or a spoiler for the campaign beyond this module.

Where the campaign goes from here

This closes the surface confrontation — the climax of Act I, not the end of the module. The party returns to Loftwick for Phase 5 (The Small Matter); the trail then runs to Greyhawk (Phase 6) and descends into the route beneath the Cairn Hills (Phases 7–9). The campaign's deepest questions — taken up across those later phases, the first two pointing beyond this module entirely — include:

  • Who is the writer of the "E." annotations? (Spoiler: Eclavdra of House Eilserv, but the campaign should never name her until and unless the party reaches the underdark.)
  • What is the older shape behind the harbor-revenue play? (The Suel-Drow long-game; the Vault of the Drow as positional asset; the slow-burning Demon Queen worship; House Eilserv's century-scale operations.)
  • Where does Haskur Vandrell go next? (To Greyhawk City, in Phase 6 (The Brass Crow), where the party learns he was “collected, not rescued.” He is a small piece, not the prize, and he is not authorially protected — capture, kill, or lose him, the campaign continues.)
  • What does Caelith do next? (Probably retire, possibly within two years; the Audit Hall's structural problems will outlive his time in office.)
  • What does Trina do next? (This is Trina's question and the GM's; it depends on the player who runs Alicia and on the campaign's appetite for fey-adjacent threads.)

The campaign continues straight on: Phase 5 (The Small Matter) opens with Caelith's letter inviting the party back to Loftwick to discuss "a small matter that may not be small." It does not begin in the underdark. It begins in a civic room in Loftwick that the party already knows; the descent waits until Phases 7–9.
